The navy of Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) announced on Saturday that a second "violating" supertanker had exploded in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a naval mine, hours after a similar incident involving another tanker.
In a statement published on the IRGC's official news outlet Sepah News, the navy said the blast caused a "huge" fire on the vessel, which was carrying over 2 million barrels of crude oil.
It said the oil tanker had turned off its GPS and radar systems and was seeking to cross the waterway through an "illegal" route, adding that the explosion occurred in the vessel's engine room and brought it to a halt.
Earlier in the day, the IRGC Navy said another "violating" supertanker seeking to transit the strait through an "unauthorized" route had suffered a "huge" explosion after hitting a naval mine.
The IRGC Navy added that the Strait of Hormuz is closed, warning that ships violating Iranian regulations in the strategic waterway will face the consequences of relying on the "terrorist US military,” according to Iran's official news agency IRNA.
Commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, October 11, 2026. 
The reported incidents come amid growing concerns over the safety of commercial shipping in the region. Qin Tian, deputy director of the Institute of Middle East Studies at the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, said attacks on commercial vessels in the strait increased significantly, particularly from late September to early October, in an interview with China Media Group.
Qin said the attacks have driven tanker freight rates to record highs and pushed up insurance costs, potentially disrupting global supply chains and international trade. He also warned that tensions in the region could escalate further as Iran and the US intensify their struggle for control of the strait, raising the risk of renewed military conflict.
Meanwhile, US military deployments and diplomatic contacts between Washington and Israel have drawn attention to the possibility of further escalation involving Iran.
The US Central Command said the aircraft carrier USS George H.W. Bush had returned to the Arabian Sea after a visit to Thailand. The carrier has approximately 5,000 sailors and other personnel on board.
Separately, Israel's Channel 12 reported that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had recently spoken by phone with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to discuss potential military action against Iran. Israeli officials have indicated that military action against Tehran remains an option. However, officials from both Israel and the United States told Channel 12 that their assessments suggested the situation had not yet reached a point requiring immediate military action.
A minibus drives past a cemetery wall displaying portraits of slain Houthi fighters in Sanaa, Yemen, October 15, 2026. 
Elsewhere in the region, fighting between Saudi Arabia-led coalition and Yemen's Houthi movement has continued, with both sides reporting military operations and attacks.
Early Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Khamis Mushait.
On Saturday, the coalition announced the interception of four drones over Riyadh and the kingdom's eastern and southern regions, while destroying two ballistic missile launchers in Yemen's northern Saada Province.
Yemen's armed forces said on Saturday they had carried out 1,417 strikes against Houthi targets over 24 hours, claiming that around 800 fighters had been killed or wounded.
As for the Houthis, the group said on Saturday that its forces shot down a Saudi Apache attack helicopter near the border region of Najran, without providing further details on the crew's fate or the exact location.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia, and the claim could not be independently verified.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said Saudi warplanes carried out 53 airstrikes in Yemen over the past 24 hours. Sarea accused the strikes of hitting civilian sites and causing casualties, including women and children, without providing a toll.

China will accelerate its green and low-carbon transition, promote the peaking of coal and oil consumption, and work to fulfill its 2030 Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), an environmental official said at a press conference on Wednesday, underscoring the country's continued efforts to address climate change.
China has made significant progress in its green and low-carbon transition. In the first half of this year, the country's installed renewable energy capacity reached 2.455 billion kilowatts, accounting for 60.7% of its total installed power generation capacity. By the end of July, installed solar power capacity had surpassed coal-fired power capacity for the first time, making it China's largest power source, said Li Gao, vice minister of ecology and environment, highlighting the country's strong momentum in green development.
Li added that China ranked first in the world in the combined installed capacity of nuclear power units in operation and those approved and under construction. The country has also ranked first globally in new energy vehicle production and sales for 11 consecutive years. It has built the world's largest and most comprehensive clean energy industrial chain, with green and low-carbon industries becoming an important driver of economic growth.
China has also strengthened its institutional system for addressing climate change, Li said.
The Ecological Environment Code, which came into force in August, includes a dedicated chapter on climate change, marking the first time China's legislation has made specific provisions on the issue.
Efforts to achieve China's "dual carbon" goals – reaching carbon peaking before 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality by 2060 – have been incorporated into central environmental protection inspections, while the green and low-carbon transformation of development approaches has been included in assessments of building a Beautiful China.
So far, China has issued 113 national standards for carbon emissions management, with more than 50 additional standards expected this year, covering areas including carbon accounting, carbon trading and carbon footprints, Li said.
Carbon market enters a new phase of growth
A digital screen showing trading activity in China's domestic carbon market in 2024. 
China has established the world's largest national carbon emissions trading market, while its voluntary greenhouse gas emissions reduction trading market continues to expand, Li noted.
The cumulative trading volume in the national carbon market recently surpassed 1 billion tonnes. The market also covered about 8.3 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions, accounting for over 65% of the country's total.
During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), China's carbon market helped reduce carbon dioxide emissions in the thermal power sector by about 530 million tonnes. It also generated around 36 billion yuan (about $5.4 billion) in emission-reduction benefits for more than 1,100 key emitting entities, and lowered the country's cumulative emission-reduction costs by 56.8 billion yuan (about $8.5 billion).
Meanwhile, China has been improving its carbon emissions statistics and accounting systems, with progress achieved in establishing the product carbon footprint management framework. The database of national greenhouse gas emission factor has been launched, while carbon management capabilities among industries and enterprises continue to improve.
